svg.title: Audio plugins I write audio plugins for music production in Rust, using nih-plug for the DSP and plugin plumbing and egui for the interface, and ship them as CLAP and VST3. Each plugin begins as one sentence about what it does. That sentence stays at the top of the design document, and I build out from it, adding features as I see fit. When a feature doesn't fit the sentence, it goes to a different plugin. I like controls that mean something physical. Corrosion asks how big the pipe is and how rusted. Once you know what a knob does to the object, you can stop reading the manual. There are no mode menus. Each plugin is one continuum, with the familiar sound as the default and the strange stuff a few turns away. Before anything is released, it passes automated tests, real-time safety checks (the audio thread never allocates memory) and the standard plugin validators. That doesn't make it bug-free, but it does catch the obvious crashes before you do. And Rust, of course, catches plenty more. Everything is free software under GPLv3. If you buy a build on Ko-fi, you're funding the next plugin and getting builds you can install straight away. In development These are at the concept stage: each has a PRD and a DSP spec, and each has to pass an offline Python prototype before any Rust gets written. Orrery: a reverb made of sound sources orbiting the listener, or a rotary speaker with forty rotors. Radius sets how far each source travels, in meters (0.30 m is a Leslie horn). Coherence sets how the orbits line up: locked pairs are a rotary speaker, evenly spread is a string ensemble, scattered is a granular cloud. Drift spreads their speeds across just intervals, from unison to a chord. Because the reverb tail is made of the same orbiting copies, the space itself rotates. Sideband: a ring modulator whose carrier follows the note you play. Ratio sets the carrier relative to that note: at simple ratios the sidebands land on just intervals, so a single note becomes a power chord or a triad; at 1 it's an octave fuzz; off the grid it's a bell. Density morphs the carrier from a sine to an impulse train, ending in a sample-rate crusher that tracks the note. Purity moves it between harmonizer and clangorous ring mod. Out of the box it's an octave fuzz. Undertow: an envelope-driven phaser and resonant filter on one modulation bus, with bipolar depth, so the filter can sweep up while the phaser sweeps down from the same note. Its flagship routing, Vortex, puts the phaser inside the filter's resonance loop, giving one filter several moving resonant peaks.

g.text: AUDIO PLUGINS
I write audio plugins for music production in Rust, using nih-plug for the DSP and plugin plumbing
and egui for the interface, and ship them as CLAP and VST3.
Each plugin begins as one sentence about what it does. That sentence stays at the top of the design
document, and I build out from it, adding features as I see fit. When a feature doesn't fit the
sentence, it goes to a different plugin.
I like controls that mean something physical. Corrosion asks how big the pipe is and how rusted.
Once you know what a knob does to the object, you can stop reading the manual.
There are no mode menus. Each plugin is one continuum, with the familiar sound as the default and
the strange stuff a few turns away.
Before anything is released, it passes automated tests, real-time safety checks (the audio thread
never allocates memory) and the standard plugin validators. That doesn't make it bug-free, but it
does catch the obvious crashes before you do. And Rust, of course, catches plenty more.
Everything is free software under GPLv3. If you buy a build on Ko-fi, you're funding the next plugin
and getting builds you can install straight away.
IN DEVELOPMENT
These are at the concept stage: each has a PRD and a DSP spec, and each has to pass an offline
Python prototype before any Rust gets written.
Orrery: a reverb made of sound sources orbiting the listener, or a rotary speaker with forty
rotors. Radius sets how far each source travels, in meters (0.30 m is a Leslie horn). Coherence
sets how the orbits line up: locked pairs are a rotary speaker, evenly spread is a string
ensemble, scattered is a granular cloud. Drift spreads their speeds across just intervals, from
unison to a chord. Because the reverb tail is made of the same orbiting copies, the space itself
rotates.
Sideband: a ring modulator whose carrier follows the note you play. Ratio sets the carrier
relative to that note: at simple ratios the sidebands land on just intervals, so a single note
becomes a power chord or a triad; at 1 it's an octave fuzz; off the grid it's a bell. Density
morphs the carrier from a sine to an impulse train, ending in a sample-rate crusher that tracks
the note. Purity moves it between harmonizer and clangorous ring mod. Out of the box it's an
octave fuzz.
Undertow: an envelope-driven phaser and resonant filter on one modulation bus, with bipolar
depth, so the filter can sweep up while the phaser sweeps down from the same note. Its flagship
routing, Vortex, puts the phaser inside the filter's resonance loop, giving one filter several
moving resonant peaks.
